```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(stablr)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw())

# A shared palette for storage temperatures, used throughout.
temp_cols <- c("5" = "navy", "25" = "darkgoldenrod2", "30" = "seagreen",
               "37" = "orange2", "40" = "red3")
```

## Introduction

`simulate_kinetic_data()` generates stability data from the kinetic models included in `stablr`.
You choose the reaction mechanism, the kinetic order, the temperature
dependence and the batch-to-batch spread; the function draws the generating
parameters, evolves the trajectories with the modified Arrhenius equation, and
adds measurement error. 

The two simulated datasets included with the package, `nrcesds` and `upsec`, were
built with this function. This vignette explains how a call is put together, begins with the simplest case, and reproduces both datasets exactly. Every call returns a **long-format** data frame with one row per (design point × measured species); the warm-up below shows the layout.


## Inputs of `simulate_kinetic_data()`

The function `simulate_kinetic_data()` has three key inputs: the **study
design**, the **mechanism**, and the **parameters**.

### Study design

| Argument | Role |
|---|---|
| `time_points` | Numeric vector of sampling times (e.g. months). |
| `temperatures_C` | Numeric vector of storage temperatures in °C. |
| `factors` | Named integer vector of extra design factors and their level counts, e.g. `c("batch" = 6)`. Optional. |
| `intercept_cols` | Which factors shift the *initial* values ($A_0$, …). |
| `rate_cols` | Which factors shift the *rate constants* and activation energies. |

The design is the full crossing of `time_points`, `temperatures_C`, and any
`factors`. A factor only alters the generating parameters when it is listed in
`intercept_cols` or `rate_cols`; named but placed in neither, it simply
replicates the design grid.

### Mechanism

| Argument | Options | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `reaction_type` | `"kinetic"`, `"single_deg"`, `"parallel"` | Track only A; A → B; or A → B and A → C. |
| `kinetic_order` | `0`, `1`, `2` | Zero-, first-, or second-order kinetics. |
| `trend` | `"increasing"`, `"decreasing"` | Whether A grows or decays. (`"parallel"` is always decreasing.) |
| `trefk` | Kelvin | Reference temperature for the Arrhenius reparameterization (default 298.15 K = 25 °C). |

Rate constants are temperature-dependent through the modified Arrhenius
equation,
$$k(T) = k_{\text{ref}} \, \exp\!\left(\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_{\text{ref}}} - \frac{1}{T} \right)\right),$$
so higher temperatures degrade faster. This is the same parameterization the
`fit_*` functions estimate.

### Parameters

`params` is a list. Every generating quantity is given as a **center** plus a
**spread**, and each is drawn from a distribution matched to its physical
support:

| Quantity | Center | Spread | Distribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial values | `A0_target` (`B0_target`, `C0_target`) | `A0_target_sd` (`0` pins to target) | Dirichlet/Beta, non-negative, sums to `A_max` (default 100) |
| Rate constants | `kref_median` (`krefB_median`, `krefC_median`) | `kref_gsd` ($\ge 1$; `1` = none) | lognormal, strictly positive |
| Activation energy | `Ea` (`EaB`, `EaC`) | — | deterministic within a factor level |
| Measurement error | `sigma_err` | — | additive noise SD per observation |

The B/C variants apply to the multi-species (`single_deg`, `parallel`) models;
see `?simulate_kinetic_data` for the full distributional detail. Two more
arguments shape the *observations*:

- `noise` — `"mass_balance"` (default) draws row-centered errors so the measured
  species still sum to `A_max`; `"independent"` draws an independent error per
  species, matching the least-squares assumption of the `fit_*` estimators. For
  a single measured species the two coincide.
- `clamp` — if `TRUE`, observed values are censored to the physical bounds
  `[A_min, A_max]` and a warning reports how many were clamped.


## Warm-up: A Simple Example

The simplest call has no factors and tracks a single attribute
(`reaction_type = "kinetic"`). Here purity decays by first-order kinetics at
three temperatures:

```{r warmup}
warmup <- simulate_kinetic_data(
  time_points    = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24),
  temperatures_C = c(5, 25, 40),
  reaction_type  = "kinetic",
  kinetic_order  = 1,
  trend          = "decreasing",
  params = list(
    A0_target    = 98,      # starting purity (%)
    A0_target_sd = 0.5,     # batch-to-batch spread on A0
    Ea           = 85000,   # activation energy (J/mol)
    kref_median  = 2.5e-4,  # rate at trefk (25 C)
    kref_gsd     = 1.05,    # geometric spread on the rate
    sigma_err    = 0.3      # measurement-error SD
  ),
  sdpt = 123
)

head(warmup)
```

The columns are:

- **any factor columns** you defined (e.g. `batch`)
- `time` — the sampling time (e.g. months)
- `temp` — storage temperature in °C, and `tempk` its value in Kelvin
- `cqa` — the name of the measured quality attribute
- `y` — the observed value.

Plotting the trajectories, the Arrhenius dependence is visible directly: the
40 °C trajectory falls steeply, 25 °C gently, and 5 °C is nearly flat over two
years.

```{r warmup-plot}
ggplot(warmup, aes(time, y, color = factor(temp))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Temperature (°C)", values = temp_cols) +
  labs(x = "Time (months)", y = "Purity (%)",
       title = "Generic first-order decay")
```


## Recreating `nrcesds`

`nrcesds` mimics data generated from non-reduced CE-SDS assay: a main peak degrading into minor
peaks, modelled as a single degradation (A → B) with second-order kinetics
across six batches and five temperatures. This is the exact call used to build
the dataset included in the package.

```{r nrcesds}
nrcesds_sim <- simulate_kinetic_data(
  factors        = c("batch" = 6),
  intercept_cols = "batch",
  time_points    = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36),
  temperatures_C = c(5, 25, 30, 37, 40),
  trefk          = 278.15,          # reference at 5 C
  reaction_type  = "single_deg",
  kinetic_order  = 2,
  trend          = "decreasing",
  params = list(
    A0_target    = 98,
    B0_target    = 2,               # A0 + B0 = A_max = 100
    A0_target_sd = 0.4,
    Ea           = 80000,
    kref_median  = 5e-4,
    kref_gsd     = 1.05,
    sigma_err    = 0.3
  ),
  component_names = list(comp_A = "NR Major Peak", comp_B = "NR Minor Peaks"),
  clamp = TRUE,
  sdpt  = 42,
  return_params = TRUE     # also keep the drawn parameters (see below)
)
```

`component_names` renames the two species, so `cqa` carries the assay's own
labels. `return_params = TRUE` returns a list with the data in `$data` and the
parameters actually drawn in `$parameters` (used in the *Peeking at the truth*
section below). Plotting the major and minor peaks side by side, with the six
batches overlaid at each temperature:

```{r nrcesds-plot, fig.height=4}
ggplot(nrcesds_sim$data, aes(time, y, color = factor(temp), group = interaction(batch, temp))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ cqa, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Temperature (°C)", values = temp_cols) +
  labs(x = "Time (months)", y = "Value (%)")
```

The result is identical to the packaged `nrcesds`:

```{r nrcesds-identical}
data(nrcesds)
all.equal(as.data.frame(nrcesds_sim$data), as.data.frame(nrcesds))
```


## Recreating `upsec`

`upsec` mimics a UPSEC assay, where the main species degrades into *two*
products simultaneously: high- and low-molecular-weight species. This is the
parallel mechanism (A → B and A → C) with first-order kinetics. The only
structural differences from `nrcesds` are `reaction_type = "parallel"`, the
first-order kinetics, and the separate `EaB`/`EaC` and `krefB`/`krefC` rate
parameters for the two pathways.

```{r upsec}
upsec_sim <- simulate_kinetic_data(
  factors        = c("batch" = 6),
  intercept_cols = "batch",
  time_points    = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36),
  temperatures_C = c(5, 25, 30, 37, 40),
  trefk          = 278.15,
  reaction_type  = "parallel",
  kinetic_order  = 1,
  trend          = "decreasing",
  params = list(
    A0_target    = 98,
    B0_target    = 0.8,
    C0_target    = 1.2,             # A0 + B0 + C0 = A_max = 100
    A0_target_sd = 0.5,
    EaB          = 85000,
    EaC          = 80000,
    krefB_median = 4e-4,
    krefB_gsd    = 1.05,
    krefC_median = 2e-4,
    krefC_gsd    = 1.05,
    sigma_err    = 0.4
  ),
  component_names = list(comp_A = "Total Main", comp_B = "HMWS", comp_C = "LMWS"),
  clamp = TRUE,
  sdpt  = 123
)
```

The `clamp = TRUE` warning reports that a couple of near-zero HMWS/LMWS
observations were censored to `[0, 100]` — expected for a minor species with
noise near the boundary. Plotting all three attributes:

```{r upsec-plot, fig.height=3.2}
ggplot(upsec_sim, aes(time, y, color = factor(temp), group = interaction(batch, temp))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ cqa, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Temperature (°C)", values = temp_cols) +
  labs(x = "Time (months)", y = "Value (%)")
```

As the Total Main species declines, the two degradants accumulate in proportion
to their relative rate constants. Again, the result matches the shipped dataset:

```{r upsec-identical}
data(upsec)
all.equal(as.data.frame(upsec_sim), as.data.frame(upsec))
```


## Peeking at the truth

The distinctive value of a simulator is that the truth is knowable. Two devices
expose it.

### The drawn parameters

Because the `nrcesds` call above was made with `return_params = TRUE`, the
parameters drawn for each factor combination are already available in
`nrcesds_sim$parameters`:

```{r return-params}
# Per-batch initial values, drawn around the targets A0 = 98, B0 = 2:
nrcesds_sim$parameters$intercept_params
```

Here only `batch` was placed in `intercept_cols`, so the initial values vary by
batch while the single rate constant (not in `rate_cols`) is shared:

```{r return-params-rate}
nrcesds_sim$parameters$rate_params
nrcesds_sim$parameters$fixed_params[c("trefk", "kinetic_order", "trend", "sigma_err")]
```

### The noise-free trajectory

To see the underlying signal beneath the measurement error, re-run the *same*
call with `sigma_err = 0` and the *same* seed. The seed fixes the parameter
draws, so the noise-free run traces the exact truth the noisy points scatter
around. Using the warm-up example:

```{r truth-overlay}
truth <- simulate_kinetic_data(
  time_points    = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24),
  temperatures_C = c(5, 25, 40),
  reaction_type  = "kinetic",
  kinetic_order  = 1,
  trend          = "decreasing",
  params = list(A0_target = 98, A0_target_sd = 0.5, Ea = 85000,
                kref_median = 2.5e-4, kref_gsd = 1.05,
                sigma_err = 0),      # <- noise switched off
  sdpt = 123                          # <- same seed as `warmup`
)

ggplot(warmup, aes(time, color = factor(temp))) +
  geom_point(aes(y = y)) +
  geom_line(data = truth, aes(y = y)) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Temperature (°C)", values = temp_cols) +
  labs(x = "Time (months)", y = "Purity (%)",
       title = "Observed points (with noise) vs. true curves (no noise)")
```

The lines are the true first-order decay; the points are those same
trajectories seen through measurement error of SD `sigma_err = 0.3`.
